questions.question: The iShares Core MSCI World ETF (IE00B4L5Y983) factsheet reports an ongoing charge. Does the KID for the same fund report a consistent ongoing cost figure?
questions.expected_answer: Yes, both report 0.20% — factsheet as Total Expense Ratio, KID as Annual cost impact or ongoing costs taken each year in What are the costs section.
questions.note: Tests cross-document consistency for the same ETF. Also a sanity check on extraction: if the two figures differ, it is likely a parsing error not a real discrepancy.

questions.question: What replication method does IE00B4L5Y983 use according to its factsheet, and does the KID description of the product mention the same approach?
questions.expected_answer: Factsheet states Physical (with Optimised methodology) product structure; KID instead does not describe the fund structure in replication terms.
questions.note: Medium: the KID rarely uses the word 'replication' — the system must interpret equivalent prose.

questions.question: The UBS Core MSCI World ETF (IE00BD4TXV59) KID describes performance scenarios. Does the factsheet's performance section tell a consistent story about expected returns?
questions.expected_answer: The KID performance scenarios are forward-looking, model-based projections under the PRIIPs framework, while the factsheet shows realised historical returns. These are not directly comparable. Although the historical returns fall within the broad range of outcomes shown in the KID, this does not imply consistency, as the central scenario represents a modelled median outcome rather than an annualised expectation derived from past performance.
questions.note: Hard: requires joining a scenario table chunk (KID) with a performance chart narrative (factsheet). Direct test of table block_type chunk retrieval.

questions.question: Compare how IE00B4L5Y983 (iShares) and IE00BD4TXV59 (UBS) each describe their target investor in their respective KIDs.
questions.expected_answer: Based on KIDs, both Funds are intended for retail investors with the ability to bear losses.
questions.note: Hard: target market description is prose-heavy and often spans multiple sentences. Tests whether 400-char KID chunks preserve enough context.
